title: Benji and the Homework Mystery
markdown:
Sunlight burst in, bright and buttery, and tickled Benji’s whiskers. Pigeons cooed a happy chattering tune. Birds chirped morning greetings. Benji stretched his paws. A big satisfying yawn bubbled up, showing his strong front teeth. Time for breakfast. Crunchy bark and tasty reeds. And then homework.

His busy nose twitched. Something felt odd. Peculiar. He padded to his workbench. Wood bits. Stone bits. All neat. There it was, just like yesterday. A smooth grey clay tablet, cool to the touch. Pressed deep into the soft clay were the morning’s arithmetic problems. Addition, subtraction, even tricky multiplications. He could practically taste the numbers. Usually so exciting.

"Again?" Benji grumbled. Tap tap. His paw hit the tablet. "This is the third day in a row. And it looks exactly the same." The same. Again. And again. He loved numbers. Loved building with them. Calculating perfect angles for his dams. But this felt too much. Too familiar. Like singing the same song without a single new note. Building the exact same dam, day after day.

He grabbed a sharp twig, ready to solve. Then he noticed something from yesterday, a tiny detail that tickled his curious mind. The way the numbers were pressed in. They were not wobbly, like his own scribbles when he was in a hurry. These were neat, deep grooves. Almost perfect. Too perfect.

"Hmm." A thoughtful sound deep in his chest. His tail flicked. Thump. A real knotty bit of business. He looked at the tablet, then out the window toward the tallest grandest pine. High up in its branches lived Star the observatory owl. Star knew everything, especially things that were old and dusty and mysterious. Star’s knowledge was vast as the night sky.

With a determined gleam in his bright eyes, Benji zipped out of his dam, a blur of brown fur and boundless energy. He dashed across the damp grass. Thump-thump-thump. Dewdrops glittered like diamonds. The air felt cool and crisp. He bounded up the rough bark of the great pine. Claws gripped tight. Up, up, up.

"Star. Star. Are you awake?" His voice was breathy from the energetic climb, echoing through the quiet morning.

A pair of enormous golden eyes blinked open from a cozy nook. Star ruffled her magnificent midnight-dark feathers. "Benji? What is all this commotion at this early hour?" Her voice was a soft hoot, calm and deep. She tilted her head, gaze sharp.

"It is the homework, Star. It is the same, same, same. And look at this tablet." He held up the clay, its surface gleaming slightly. "It is so pressed in. And it is all the same numbers."

Star glided down, landing silently. She peered intently at the tablet, bright eyes narrowing. "Oh, my dear Benji. This is not new clay. Not at all. This is something much older."

"It is not?" Benji’s ears perked. His nose twitched with renewed curiosity. "What do you mean? What is it?"

"This is a clay tablet, just like the ancient scribes used, long, long ago. They would press their important messages, their stories, their numbers, into wet clay. When the clay dried hard, the writing was there forever. It is how we know so much about the brave explorers and wise builders of the past. A time capsule."

Benji’s eyes darted back to his tablet. His beaver brain whirred. "So someone pressed the homework again into this clay? But why is it the same? Why did they not press new numbers?"

Star gave a wise little nod, feathers shimmering. "Look very closely. Do you see how the marks are identical? Perfectly placed, perfectly deep?"

Benji squinted, brow furrowing. He nudged the tablet closer, turning it this way and that in the bright morning sun. The marks were identical. Perfect little numbers, lined up neatly. Each one looked exactly like the last.

"Ancient scribes were incredibly clever," Star continued, voice hushed with wonder. "To save time, or make many copies, they discovered something amazing. They would press their original writing into wet clay. Then, before that first piece dried hard, they would take another piece of wet clay and press it right onto the first one. The original writing would transfer, making a perfect identical copy."

"A copy." Benji’s tail thumped a happy excited beat against the branch. "So my homework is not new at all. It is just copies of old homework, pressed over and over again." Not a mistake. A brilliant trick.

Star hooted with delight, a soft happy sound. "Precisely. Someone, or perhaps something, is pressing copies of the same homework onto fresh clay each morning. A brilliant, if slightly repetitive, trick indeed."

Benji grinned, a wide happy beaver grin that stretched from ear to ear. He looked at his tablet with new eyes. It was not just homework anymore. It was a piece of history, a clever bit of ancient technology, a testament to the smarts of people who lived long ago.

"That is amazing. Thank you, Star. You are the best." He felt a burst of unstoppable energy, an urge to learn more, to build new things, to tackle new problems with this same kind of clever thinking.

He scampered down the tree, paws barely touching the ground, a happy trail of displaced bark in his wake. The sun was climbing higher, painting the world in golden yellows, bright blues, and fresh greens. The morning air felt alive with promise. With a grin as wide as the river, Benji raced out, ready for whatever numbers, old or new, came next.
